title: Electromechanical modelling of piezoelectric vibration energy harvester with a novel dynamic magnifier

sections.heading: Electromechanical modelling of piezoelectric vibration energy harvester with a novel dynamic magnifer
sections.text:
Elektromechanische Modellierung eines piezoelektrischen Vibrationsenergie-Harvesters mit einer neuartigen dynamischen Lupe

https://doi.org/10.1515/teme-2020-0030   
Received April 27, 2020; accepted July 8, 2020

Abstract: In piezoelectric energy harvesting devices, the relative displacement between the two ends of the harvester beam decides the output power from the piezoelectric patch. A novel four bar mechanism with a helical spring is used as a dynamic magnifer to improve the relative displacement and thereby the output power from the harvester. This dynamic magnifer is placed between the base excitation location and the composite harvester beam to form two degrees of freedom (2DOF) piezoelectric energy harvester. Electromechanical coupled analytical equations for the voltage and output power are derived using a lumped electromechanical model. The model is developed assuming linear transverse vibrations of the harvester. A dynamic magnifer is fabricated for the required frequency range and the suitable dimensions of the harvester beam are estimated using commercially available software. Experiments are conducted for base excitation amplitude of $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ and the performance of the proposed 2DOF harvester is studied for the output voltage and power. The proposed 2DOF harvester has shown $1 1 0 \%$ improvement in output power in frst mode and $2 7 0 \%$ improvement in second mode compared to the conventional single degree of freedom (SDOF) cantilevered harvester for given identical input conditions. The measured frequencies and output power are validated with analytical solutions and are found to be in good agreement. Further, the efect of mass ratio, stifness ratio and base excitation amplitude on the output voltage and power is investigated using analytical expressions.

Keywords: Electromechanical model, dynamic magnifer, 2DOF harvester, composite harvester beam, macro fber composite, piezoelectric efect.

Zusammenfassung: Bei piezoelektrischen Energy Harvestern bestimmt unter anderem die relative Verschiebung zwischen den beiden Enden des Biegebalkens die erzielbare Ausgangsleistung. Ein Gelenkmechanismus mit einer Feder wird als dynamischer Verstärker verwendet, um den Schwingweg, also die Auslenkung des Biegebalkens und damit die Ausgangsleistung des Harvesters zu verbessern. Dieses schwingungsfähige System wird zwischen der Anregung und dem eigentlichen Harvester positioniert und bildet ein System mit zwei Freiheitsgraden (2DOF). Für dieses elektromechanisch gekoppelte System werden die analytischen Gleichungen sowohl für die Spannung als auch die Ausgangsleistung unter Verwendung eines Modells mit konzentrierten Parametern abgeleitet. Der dem Harvester vorgeschaltete Resonator wird auf den geforderten Frequenzbereich abgestimmt und die Abmessungen des Biegebalkens des Harvesters werden durch Simulation ermittelt. Für Anregeamplituden von $_ { 0 , 0 5 \mathrm { m m } }$ werden über Experimente die Ausgangsleistung und auch die Ausgangsspannung messtechnisch ermittelt. Gegenüber herkömmlichen Systemen ergibt sich für die vorgeschlagene Anordnung eine Steigerung der Ausgangsleistung von $1 1 0 \%$ für die erste Resonanzfrequenz bzw. $2 7 0 \%$ für die zweiten Resonanzfrequenz (verglichen mit einfachen Systemen ohne vorgeschalteten Resonator). Die gemessenen Resonanzfrequenzen und Ausgangsleistungen werden mit analytischen Lösungen verglichen und es zeigt sich eine gute Übereinstimmung. Ferner wird unter Verwendung analytischer Ausdrücke die Auswirkung der Federsteifgkeit und der Resonatormasse auf die Ausgangsspannung und Ausgangsleistung untersucht.

Schlagwörter: Elektromechanisches Modell, dynamische Verstärkung, 2DOF-energy Harvester, zusammengesetzter Biegebalken, piezoelektrischer Efekt, Makrofaserverbundwerkstof.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Wireless sensor technologies have recently found extensive applications because of the low cost of installation. New trends in digital signal processing have reduced the power needed to operate wireless sensors. The wireless sensor applications are wide spread, for example in natural environmental monitoring, process monitoring, animal tracking and safety, control, security and surveillance, supply chain control, structural health monitoring, agricultural automation, building environment control, identifcation and personalisation, smart homes, warehouse inventory, etc. [1, 2]. These sensors are usually operated by batteries and these batteries have a limited life of operation and are non-ecofriendly. Structures like buildings, bridges, etc. are usually susceptible to low frequency vibrations. The concept of converting vibration energy into electrical energy appears to have initially been proposed by Williams and Yates [3]. Roundy et al. [4] stated that the piezoelectric conversion mechanism has shown superior performance in terms of robustness and power density and needs simpler electronics in comparison to electromagnetic and electrostatic conversion mechanisms. Erturk and Daniel [5] developed a single degree of freedom (SDOF) distributed electromechanical model for the power output from a cantilevered piezoelectric energy harvester. The SDOF cantilevered harvester has limitations with respect to bandwidth and output power. A small shift in the vibrations of the input host structure reduces the output power from the harvester drastically [6]. To deal with this issue, a large number of researchers have studied various mechanical features of the harvester. These features can be broadly classifed into tuning technique, confguration technique, dual mode technique and nonlinear technique.

The concept of a dynamic vibration absorber (DVA) applied to a 2DOF harvester appears to have been initially been used by Cornwell et al. [7]. The dual mode harvesters developed by Erturk et al. [8]. Ma et al. [9], Arafa et al. [10] could not be regarded as truly broadband as the two resonances were quite far away from each other [6]. Ali and Adhikari [11] developed a model to control the vibrations of the host structure by attaching a DVA which was augmented with a piezoelectric stack to harvest vibration energy. Wu et al. [6] developed a cut-out beam type 2DOF piezoelectric energy harvester did not show any signifcant improvement in the output voltage over an SDOF harvester. Obtaining improved power output with close natural frequencies and a comparatively simple dynamic magnifer is a challenging task and is attempted in this paper.

In a previous paper [12] the authors have carried out preliminary investigations of the proposed harvester. Initially, the performance of the proposed 2DOF harvester was simulated using a commercial dynamic analysis software and these were validated with experimental results and found to be in good agreement. The current paper focuses on deriving linear lumped electromechanical analytical expressions for relative displacement, output voltage and power. The experimental results in [12] are now validated by analytical solutions; thereafter a parametric study is carried out using analytical expressions. It is shown that the analytical model correctly represents the output behaviour of the proposed 2DOF harvester. This model is useful for the design and optimization of the proposed 2DOF harvester (2DOFH).

sections.heading: 2 Analytical modelling of four bar mechanism 2DOF harvester
sections.text:
Figure 1(a) shows a schematic of the proposed four bar mechanism 2DOF harvester with electrical circuit. It consists of three major parts viz., primary system, secondary system and electrical circuit. The primary system consists of a four bar mechanism and a helical spring to act as an elastic dynamic magnifer. The secondary system consists of a composite harvester beam with a tip mass. The composite harvester beam is formed by bonding a macro fber composite (MFC) piezoelectric patch to a copper substructure. Electrical circuit consisting of variable resistor is connected across the output terminals of the MFC to measure the output voltage from the harvester. The primary and secondary systems are combined to form a 2DOF harvester. This harvester system is mounted on a vibrating host structure. The vibrations from the host structure are transferred to the primary system, which gives an amplifed vibration input to the harvester beam. The relative displacement between the two ends of the harvester beam induces strain in the substructure beam and this is transferred to the active piezoelectric MFC. By virtue of the direct piezoelectric efect, the induced strain in the beam produces an output voltage from the MFC.

The equivalent lumped model of the 2DOF harvester is as shown in Fig. 1(b), and is used to derive the theoretical electromechanical coupled equations for relative displacements, output voltage and power. The primary system is modelled as equivalent mass $m _ { 1 }$ , spring with stifness $k _ { 1 }$ and damper with damping coefcient $c _ { 1 }$ . The secondary system is modelled as equivalent mass $m _ { 2 }$ , spring with stifness $k _ { 2 }$ , damper with damping coefcient $c _ { 2 }$ and electromechanical coupling coefcient $\theta _ { p }$ . The displacement of the host structure vibration is denoted by $y _ { g }$ and is assumed as transverse harmonic.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental setup
sections.text: This section contains details regarding the design and fabrication of the primary and secondary systems and experimental setup.

sections.heading: 3.1 Design of primary system (four bar mechanism with helical spring)
sections.text:
The cantilevered type piezoelectric energy harvester needs in-plane transverse vibrations. The four bar mechanism with the spring as a dynamic magnifer produces in-plane transverse vibrations with almost negligible amplitude in the other two directions. Accordingly, the proposed dynamic magnifer (primary system) is designed to obtain a natural frequency between $2 5 \mathrm { H z }$ and $3 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Figure 2(a)

shows the design drawing of the four bar mechanism. This mechanism is fabricated by using stif SS304 material and the helical spring using spring steel. Machined brass material bars are used to act as pins at hinge joints. Figure 2(b) shows the displaced position of the horizontal link by an arbitrary angle of $1 0 ^ { \circ }$ . The transverse and horizontal displacements are measured as $7 . 8 2 \mathrm { m m }$ and $0 . 6 \mathrm { m m }$ respectively. This ensures that the proposed 1:1 four bar mechanism confguration gives in plane transverse displacement with negligible horizontal displacement, as is required for the harvester beam. Figure 2(c) shows a picture of the fabricated four bar mechanism. The vibration response of the primary system is measured by using Dytran make 3053 triaxial accelerometer. Figure 2(d) shows the free vibration test response. The measured natural frequency and damping ratio of the primary system are found to be $2 6 . 7 5 \mathrm { H z }$ and 0.026 respectively. Experiments show good repeatability and these results are the average values obtained over 5 trials. This damping factor includes also friction in hinges and this friction is not a signifcant problem in functioning of this proposed mechanism.

![](images/fd86fa77164adb6557b66477583a6f305559afb97166c079a30cd6eddb22f38a.jpg)  
Figure 3: First mode behaviour of harvester beam in COMSOL Multiphysics 3a.

![](images/9fa77f945b4591ec1bc07332298931f0be66f57db832d076148662fa5dba06e3.jpg)  
Figure 4: Harvester beam for experiments.

sections.heading: 3.2 Design of secondary system (harvester beam)
sections.text:
A harvester beam is formed by bonding a piezoelectric patch on to a substructure beam with a tip mass. The relative displacement between the two ends of the harvester beam decides the output voltage from the harvester. The strain is maximum near the fxed end in cantilevered type harvester beam arrangement. Hence the piezoelectric patch is pasted on the substructure near the fxed end to achieve maximum output voltage. A higher elastic modulus of the harvester beam will reduce the strain (output voltage) induced in the harvester beam [7]. Hence a secondary system with lower elastic modulus is built by using a copper plate to fabricate the substructure and the MFC as piezoelectric material.

Eigenfrequency analysis is performed in COMSOL Multiphysics 3a software to estimate the dimensions of the substructure beam with the following specifcations. Overall dimensions of the MFC: $3 7 \times 1 8 \times 0 . 3 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ ; active dimensions of the MFC: $2 8 \times 1 4 \times 0 . 3 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , tip mass: $0 . 5 8 { \tt g }$ Figure 3 shows the model of the harvester beam with the MFC pasted over the copper substructure with active dimensions. The size of the copper substructure of dimensions $1 0 9 . 5 \times 1 7 . 5 \times 0 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ gives the frst mode frequency as $2 4 . 3 \mathrm { H z }$ .

The harvester beam is fabricated in accordance with the simulations and the fabricated harvester beam is shown in Fig. 4. The measured frst mode natural frequency of the fabricated harvester beam is found to be 27.95 Hz. There is a diference of $3 . 6 4 \mathrm { H z }$ between the measured and simulated frst mode natural frequency of the harvester beam. The stifness of the fabricated harvester beam could perhaps have increased because the MFC is bonded over the substructure for the overall dimensions. This in turn could have increased the natural frequency of the harvester beam. This harvester beam (secondary system) is clamped in the fxtures of the four bar mechanism (primary system) in cantilevered arrangement to act as a 2DOF harvester. Figure 5 shows the experimental setup established in the laboratory. The 2DOF harvester is mounted on a cam and follower type mechanical shaker for testing.

To assess the output power from the harvester, steady state forced vibration test is performed with a harmonic base excitation of $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . During the forward sweep, the frequency is swept from $1 \mathrm { H z }$ to $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ and from $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ to 1 Hz during the reverse sweep. With the harvester operating at its resonance frequency, the electrical load resistance is changed from $1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Experimental study of SDOF harvester
sections.text: The harvester beam shown in Fig. 4 is mounted on a shaker table with cantilever fxtures (without dynamic magnifer mechanism). Since frst mode is signifcant in this arrangement, here onwards this arrangement is called as SDOF harvester. The experimental performance of SDOF harvester is studied for the conditions mentioned in the section 3.2. Figure 6(a) shows the plot of open circuit voltage vs. frequency. The maximum value of open circuit voltage at resonant frequency of $2 7 . 9 5 \mathrm { H z }$ is measured as $2 4 \mathrm { V } .$ Figure 6(b) shows the plot of power vs. electrical resistance. The measured maximum value of power is $0 . 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at a resistance of $2 3 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ .

sections.heading: 4.1.2 Experimental study of 2DOF harvester
sections.text:
The same harvester beam (secondary system) is fxed in fxtures provided in four bar mechanism (primary system) to act as 2DOF harvester. The experiments are performed with the conditions as that for SDOF harvester. Figure 7 shows the results obtained from experiments with 2DOF harvester. Figure 7(a) shows the open circuit vs. frequency plot. The measured frequency and voltage in the frst mode are $2 5 . 6 4 \mathrm { H z }$ and $3 4 . 8 \mathrm { V }$ and $3 0 . 0 3 \mathrm { H z }$ and $4 1 . 3 \mathrm { V }$ in the second mode. The output voltage from 2DOF harvester increases by $4 5 \%$ in the frst mode and by $7 2 \%$ in the second mode when compared to SDOF harvester for the same given identical input conditions. The output voltage readings are taken in two ways; i) keeping operating frequency constant, electrical resistance is changed from $1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $1 0 0 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and ii) keeping constant electrical resistance, frequency is swept from $1 \mathrm { H z }$ to $4 0 \mathrm { H z }$ . Figures 7(b) and (c) show power vs. electrical load resistance plots at the frst and second modes respectively taken from the frst method. The maximum power in the frst mode is measured as $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 . 1 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 5 2 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in the second mode. In second method, experiments are performed at selected constant electrical resistance of $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and frequency is swept in the region as mentioned earlier. Figure 7(d) shows power vs. resistance plot, output power obtained at frst mode is $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { m W }$ and $1 . 1 1 \mathrm { m W }$ at second mode. When compared to SDOF harvester, the output power from 2DOF harvester is improved by $1 1 0 \%$ in the frst mode and by $2 7 0 \%$ in the second mode. Apart from peaks, the measured power at anti-resonance is found to $0 . 0 7 6 \mathrm { m W } .$

![](images/4a515626d6c80643e3864638fb2b0fdf2a0d9381812582b5cfbfe63341cdd818.jpg)  
Figure 7: Measured (a) open circuit voltage (b) displacement at tip (c) power at mode1 (d) power at mode2.

sections.heading: 4.2 Analytical study
sections.text:
Initially analytical studies are conducted to validate the experimental results of 2DOF harvester. The measured frequency and output power in the frst and second modes are validated with the analytical model. From equation (7), the closed circuit voltage vs. frequency curves are plotted for diferent values of electrical load resistance and are as shown in Fig. 8(a). With increase in the electrical load resistance from $5 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $2 5 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ , the closed circuit output voltage increases. The frequency in the frst mode is found to be $2 5 . 4 6 \mathrm { H z }$ and $2 8 . 3 6 \mathrm { H z }$ in the second mode. From equation (12), power vs. resistance curves in the frst and second modes are plotted and are as shown in Fig. 8(b). As the electrical load resistance increases, the output power increases up to a certain value of electrical load resistance; it decreases afterwards with increasing electrical load resistance. These trends are similar to the one obtained from experiments as shown in Figs. 7(b) and (c). The maximum predicted value of power in the frst mode $\left( 2 5 . 4 6 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ is found to be $0 . 9 6 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 4 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 . 0 4 \mathrm { m W }$ at $1 3 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in the second mode $\left( 2 8 . 3 6 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ , whereas the measured power in the frst mode $\left( 2 5 . 6 4 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ is $0 . 6 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 1 0 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 . 1 3 \mathrm { m W }$ at $2 5 2 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ in the second mode $\left( 3 0 . 0 3 \mathrm { H z } \right)$ .

![](images/6beceb082a86b3569fbe2b7e591bb846657422ca5cb80821ed5a0f4cf4981056.jpg)  
Figure 8: 2DOF harvester (a) Closed circuit voltage (b) power at frst and second mode, using analytical model.

![](images/97ffa145da76b188e317f397d967b97dfa46a2a796b8eae49c4dfae93f4eee34.jpg)  
Figure 9: Trend of output power with respect to electrical load resistance and frequency ratio.

The power will be maximum for a particular value of operating frequency and electrical load resistance. Figure 9 is a 3D plot showing the trend of output power with respect to electrical load resistance and frequency ratio. The optimum electrical resistance to achieve the maximum power is given by the equation $R = 1 / ( \omega C _ { p } )$ [13]. From this equation it can be said that as operating frequency increases, the required optimum electrical load resistance decreases. This trend is observed both in the measured and analytical studies. The experimentally measured and analytically predicted frst and second mode frequencies and power values are in reasonable agreement. These small deviations may be due to modelling assumptions and experimental errors. However, noticeable deviations in measured and analytically predicted optimum electrical load resistance values are observed, also seen in literature [14].

![](images/3fb8b46e96f05315ce2272ed43c3ccf53403aba3094580526bff6e8e0641e570.jpg)  
Figure 10: Efect of mass ratio on (a) closed circuit voltage (b) zoom-in view of closed circuit voltage (c) output power; (d) output power vs. mass ratio trend.

sections.heading: 4.3 Parametric study
sections.text:
peak voltage in the frst mode decreases and that in the second mode increases by a small margin. With a decrease in operating frequency from $3 6 . 7 2 \mathrm { H z }$ to $1 7 . 6 8 \mathrm { H z }$ , the required optimum electrical load resistance increases from $1 0 4 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ to $2 1 3 \mathrm { k } \Omega$ . Decreasing the mass ratio reduces the output power due to an increase in the required optimum electrical load resistance, even though there is a marginal increase in the output voltage and this trend is shown in Fig. 10(c). The trend in output power with change in mass ratio is as shown in Fig. 10(d).

Since the measured and analytical results are in reasonable agreement, a further parametric study is carried out by using analytical equations. The efect of mass ratio, stifness ratio and base excitation on the output power from the 2DOF harvester is investigated. The mass ratio is given by the ratio of the equivalent mass of the harvester beam to the mass of the dynamic magnifer. The stifness ratio is given by the ratio of equivalent stifness of the secondary system (harvester beam) to the equivalent stifness of the primary system (dynamic magnifer/four bar mechanism and helical spring).

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Efect of mass ratio $( \mu = m _ { 2 } / m _ { 1 } )$
sections.text:
This study is carried out for diferent mass ratios, viz., 0.05, 0.0104 and 0.0174, keeping a constant stifness ratio of 0.0124. As the mass ratio is decreased (increase in magnifer mass), the peak frequencies of the frst and second modes decrease and the frequency gap between the two modes also decreases as shown in Figs. 10(a) and (b). This study is conducted for diferent values of stifness ratios, viz., 0.0075, 0.0120 and 0.0220, keeping a constant mass ratio of 0.0104. As the stifness ratio is decreased (increase in magnifer stifness) the frequencies of the frst and second modes increase and the frequency gap between the two modes decreases as shown in Figs. 11(a) and (b). A noticeable increase in the output voltage is observed both in the frst and second modes as seen in Fig. 11(c). The output power from the 2DOF harvester increases both in the frst and second modes as shown in Fig. 11(d). Increase in the magnifer stifness increases the output power from the 2DOF harvester and this agrees with the statement of Cornwell et al. [7]. The trend in output power with change in stifness ratio is as shown in Fig. 11(d).

Figure 12 shows the superimposed plots of power vs. frequency for diferent mass ratio and stifness ratio. At lower operating frequencies, it is observed that a mass ratio of 0.005 produces a higher output power and closer frst two mode frequencies in comparison to a stifness ratio of 0.022. Similarly, at higher operating frequencies, a stifness ratio of 0.0075 produces higher output power and closer frst two mode frequencies in comparison to a mass ratio of 0.0174.

sections.text:
The efect of base excitation on the output power from the 2DOF harvester is studied for diferent base excitations from $0 . 0 1 \mathrm { m m }$ to $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { m m }$ . Figure 13(a) shows that with increase in the input base excitation, the output power increases for the entire range of operating frequencies. Figures 13(b) and (c) show the trend in output power at mode1 and mode2 with respect to base excitation.

Figure 13: Efect of base excitation on (a) power vs. frequency (b) power at mode1 (c) power at mode2.

Overall, the above studies suggest that the four bar mechanism can be efectively used as a dynamic magnifer to improve the output power from the piezoelectric energy harvester. A lumped electromechanical model has shown reasonable agreement with the experimental results for peak frequencies and output power, except for the optimal electrical load resistance and this trend is observed in literature also [14]. The proposed 2DOF harvester has shown superior performance over standalone cantilevered harvester (SDOF harvester). Further, a parametric study is conducted by using analytical equations for diferent mass and stifness ratios and base excitations.

Further by using analytical equations, the performance of the proposed 2DOF harvester is investigated for diferent mass ratios, stifness ratios and base excitations. It is observed that a higher stifness of the primary system (dynamic magnifer) gives higher output power from the 2DOF harvester. The analytical model is useful for the design and optimization of the proposed 2DOF harvester.

sections.text: This paper presents a 2DOF piezoelectric vibration energy harvester with a novel four bar mechanism and helical spring as dynamic magnifer.
